items.title: Section: Wrong Livelihood — Five Classical Forms of Dishonest Solicitation

items.zh: 若諸菩薩安住菩薩淨戒律儀，生起詭詐、虛談、現相，方便研求，假利求利，味邪命法，無有羞恥，堅持不捨，是名有犯，有所違越，是染違犯。無違犯者，若為除遣生起樂欲，發勤精進，煩惱熾盛蔽抑其心，時時現起。
items.en: Bodhisattvas abiding in the bodhisattva precepts who resort to deceptive posturing, false claims, staged appearances, badgering pressure, or shaming manipulation for gain, and who indulge this dishonest livelihood without any shame, holding fast to it and refusing to give it up — this constitutes a violation, a transgression, and it is a tainted violation. ... There is no violation for one who genuinely wishes to eliminate the pattern and applies diligent effort towards doing so, even if the affliction is so intense that it still, from time to time, overpowers and obscures the mind and recurs.

items.title: Section: Restlessness and Frivolous Conduct — Loud Laughter, Games, and Horseplay

items.zh: 若諸菩薩安住菩薩淨戒律儀，為掉所動，心不寂靜，不樂寂靜，高聲嬉戲，諠譁紛聒，輕躁騰躍，望他歡笑，如此諸緣，是名有犯，有所違越，是染違犯。若忘念起，非染違犯。無違犯者，若為除遣生起樂欲，廣說如前；若欲方便解他所生嫌恨令息；若欲遣他所生愁惱；若他性好如上諸事，方便攝受，敬慎將護，隨彼而轉；若他有情猜阻菩薩，內懷嫌恨，惡謀憎背，外現歡顏表內清淨；如是一切，皆無違犯。
items.en: Bodhisattvas abiding in the bodhisattva precepts who, stirred by restlessness, cannot find a settled mind, take no pleasure in stillness, and instead indulge in loud laughter, noisy games, boisterous commotion, and reckless, playful horseplay purely to draw out others' laughter — all such conduct constitutes a violation, a transgression, and it is a tainted violation. If it arises merely from a lapse of mindfulness, it is a non-tainted violation. ... There is no violation: for one genuinely working to eliminate the pattern, as described earlier; for one skilfully using such behaviour to dissolve another's resentment or grudge; for one seeking to relieve another's grief and distress; for one whose companion is simply inclined by nature to such things, and who joins in respectfully and carefully in order to protect the relationship and stay connected to them; and for one who, sensing that another secretly harbours suspicion, resentment, or even ill intent, nonetheless displays an outwardly cheerful face precisely to show that their own heart remains genuinely undisturbed and clear. In all such cases, there is no violation whatsoever.

items.title: Section: The Wrong View That a Bodhisattva Should Turn Away from Nirvana

items.zh: 若諸菩薩安住菩薩淨戒律儀，起如是見，立如是論：菩薩不應忻樂涅槃，應於涅槃而生厭背；於諸煩惱及隨煩惱不應怖畏而求斷滅，不應一向心生厭離；以諸菩薩三無數劫流轉生死，求大菩提。若作此說，是名有犯，有所違越，是染違犯。何以故？如諸聲聞於其涅槃忻樂親近，於諸煩惱及隨煩惱深心厭離；如是菩薩於大涅槃忻樂親近，於諸煩惱及隨煩惱深心厭離，其倍過彼百千俱胝。以諸聲聞唯為一身證得義利勤修正行，菩薩普為一切有情證得義利勤修正行。是故菩薩當勤修集無雜染心，於有漏事隨順而行，成就勝出諸阿羅漢無雜染法。
items.en: Bodhisattvas abiding in the bodhisattva precepts who form and propound the view that bodhisattvas should not delight in nirvana but should feel aversion towards it, and should not fear the afflictions and seek to eliminate them, and should not turn wholly away from them, on the grounds that bodhisattvas must pass three incalculable eons wandering through birth and death in pursuit of supreme awakening — anyone who teaches this commits a violation, a transgression, and it is a tainted violation. Why is this so? Just as śrāvakas delight in and draw near to nirvana, and turn deeply away from the afflictions, so too do bodhisattvas delight in and draw near to great nirvana, and turn deeply away from the afflictions — and do so a hundred-thousand-koti times more intensely than śrāvakas. For śrāvakas diligently cultivate the true path in pursuit of benefit for one body alone, while bodhisattvas diligently cultivate the true path in pursuit of benefit for every being universally. A bodhisattva must therefore diligently cultivate a mind free of defilement, act in accordance with worldly, conditioned affairs, and thereby accomplish an undefiled quality that surpasses even that of the arhats.

items.title: Section: Failing to Address a Slander That Is Actually True

items.zh: 若諸菩薩安住菩薩淨戒律儀，於自能發不信重言，所謂惡聲、惡稱、惡譽，不護不雪。其事若實而不避護，是名有犯，有所違越，是染違犯。若事不實而不清雪，是名有犯，有所違越，非染違犯。無違犯者，若他外道；若他憎嫉；若自出家，因行乞行、因修善行，謗聲流布，若忿蔽者；若心倒者；謗聲流布，皆無違犯。
items.en: Bodhisattvas abiding in the bodhisattva precepts who give rise, through their own conduct, to words that undermine others' trust and respect — harsh talk, harsh reputation, harsh renown — and who neither guard against it nor clear it up, commit, if the underlying accusation is in fact true and they still fail to guard against it, a violation, a transgression, and it is a tainted violation. If the accusation is false and they simply fail to clear it up, this too constitutes a violation and a transgression, but it is a non-tainted violation. ... There is no violation whatsoever: when the slanderer is a non-Buddhist outsider; when the slanderer is simply jealous; when the rumour arises from the bodhisattva's own ordained life of begging for alms or diligent spiritual practice, which naturally attracts misunderstanding; when the slanderer acts from sheer malice and bad character; or when the slanderer's mind is simply deranged.

items.title: Section: Withholding Deserved Harsh Correction Out of Misplaced Kindness — Discipline-Progression Closes

items.zh: 若諸菩薩安住菩薩淨戒律儀，見諸有情，應以種種辛楚加行、猛利加行而得義利，護其憂惱而不現行，是名有犯，有所違越，非染違犯。無違犯者，觀由此緣，於現法中少得義利，多生憂惱。
items.en: Bodhisattvas abiding in the bodhisattva precepts who see that certain beings would genuinely benefit from stern bodily discipline or forceful verbal correction, but who, wishing only to spare them distress, withhold such correction and fail to act — this constitutes a violation, a transgression, though it is a non-tainted violation. ... There is no violation when the bodhisattva judges that, in this particular case, such correction would bring about very little genuine benefit in this present life while giving rise to a great deal of needless distress and resentment instead.

items.title: Section: The Patience-Progression Cluster Opens — Returning Abuse with Abuse

items.zh: 若諸菩薩安住菩薩淨戒律儀，他罵報罵，他瞋報瞋，他打報打，他弄報弄，是名有犯，有所違越，是染違犯。
items.en: Bodhisattvas abiding in the bodhisattva precepts who, when abused, abuse in return; when met with anger, respond with anger; when struck, strike back; when mocked, mock in return — this constitutes a violation, a transgression, and it is a tainted violation.

items.title: Section: Refusing to Apologise — Pride Versus Mere Laziness

items.zh: 若諸菩薩安住菩薩淨戒律儀，於他有情有所侵犯，或自不為彼疑侵犯，由嫌嫉心，由慢所執，不如理謝而生輕捨，是名有犯，有所違越，是染違犯。若由嬾惰、懈怠、放逸，不謝輕捨，是名有犯，有所違越，非染違犯。無違犯者，若欲方便調彼、伏彼，出不善處安立善處；若是外道；若彼悕望要因現行非法有罪方受悔謝，若彼有情性好鬪諍，因悔謝時倍增憤怒；若復知彼為性堪忍體無嫌恨；若必了他因謝侵犯，深生羞恥；而不悔謝，皆無違犯。
items.en: Bodhisattvas abiding in the bodhisattva precepts who have genuinely wronged another being, or are simply suspected of having done so, and who, gripped by resentment or by pride, fail to apologise properly and instead dismiss the matter with contempt — this constitutes a violation, a transgression, and it is a tainted violation. If the failure to apologise and the contemptuous dismissal arise instead merely from laziness, carelessness, or negligence, this too constitutes a violation and a transgression, but it is a non-tainted violation. ... There is no violation: when the bodhisattva withholds the apology purely as a skilful means to guide and subdue the other, drawing them out of an unwholesome place and into a wholesome one; when the other is a non-Buddhist outsider [demanding a genuinely improper concession as the price of accepting an apology]; when the other genuinely delights in conflict, and apologising would only double their anger; when the bodhisattva knows the other is by nature genuinely tolerant and holds no resentment at all; or when the bodhisattva is certain the other would feel deep embarrassment at being formally apologised to — in all such cases, there is no violation.

blocks.text: The last precepts concerning discipline, then those concerning patience.
"Deceptive posturing, false claims, staged appearances, badgering, or shaming for gain", without shame: tainted. Venerable Miào Jìng: deceit within, false talk without.
"Loud laughter, noisy games, horseplay", stirring others to restlessness: an offence. Master Cháng Bǎi: restlessness often comes from recalling past pleasures.

Teaching that "bodhisattvas should not delight in nirvāṇa but turn from it" is an offence. "Bodhisattvas delight in great nirvāṇa and turn from afflictions far more than śrāvakas do." Master Cháng Bǎi: they only forbear from realising it in order to save beings.
If one's own conduct gives rise to a bad reputation that is deserved, and one does nothing to correct it, it is an offence.

Seeing that someone needs stern correction, and withholding it "wishing only to spare them distress", is an untainted offence. Master Cháng Bǎi: like making a novice kneel for the length of an incense stick.

"When abused, abusing in return; met with anger, angry; struck, striking back; mocked, mocking": a tainted offence. Master Cháng Bǎi: this is the Sahā world, "the world of endurance"; much that is unpleasant must be borne.

Having wronged someone, "or simply being suspected of it", and failing to apologise from pride is tainted; from laziness, untainted. No offence if apologising would only embarrass the other. Master Cháng Bǎi: an apology made with pride is not a real apology.

quiz.q: Which forms of wrong livelihood does the treatise list?
options: deceptive posturing, false talk, staged appearances, persistent pressing, and seeking gain through gain
quiz.why: "Resort to deceptive posturing, false claims, staged appearances, badgering pressure, or shaming manipulation for gain … this constitutes a tainted violation." Master Cháng Bǎi: the śrāvaka ground (fascicle 22) describes five kinds of wrong livelihood.

quiz.q: How does Venerable Miào Jìng distinguish "guǐzhà," "xūtán," and "xiànxiàng," and explain "yán"?
options: guǐzhà is inner, xūtán its outward expression; xiànxiàng concerns the body, xūtán speech; "yán" means not stopping until one gets what one wants
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: guǐzhà is inward; its outward expression is xūtán. Xiànxiàng concerns the body; xūtán is speech. "Yán" means not stopping until the goal is reached.

quiz.q: Boisterous horseplay out of restlessness — if it arises from forgetfulness, how is it judged?
quiz.why: Such conduct is a tainted violation; "if it arises from forgetfulness," untainted. Venerable Miào Jìng: "fēn" means disorder.

quiz.q: Holding that "bodhisattvas should not delight in nirvāṇa" is tainted. How does the treatise compare the bodhisattva's delight in great nirvāṇa with the śrāvaka's?
options: bodhisattvas delight in great nirvāṇa and turn from afflictions hundreds of thousands of koṭis more than śrāvakas
quiz.why: Bodhisattvas delight in great nirvāṇa and turn deeply from afflictions "hundreds of thousands of koṭis" more than śrāvakas. Venerable Miào Jìng: great nirvāṇa is non-abiding nirvāṇa.

quiz.q: What is wrong with the view that bodhisattvas should not delight in nirvāṇa? How do the lectures describe the bodhisattva's middle way?
options: both: stay in saṃsāra without practice

Cháng Bǎi: bodhisattvas forbear from realising it to save beings — otherwise it becomes compassion tainted by craving and views; Miào Jìng: not abiding in nirvāṇa is great compassion, not abiding in saṃsāra is perfect wisdom
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: the bodhisattva only forbears from realising it in order to save beings; otherwise one becomes a bodhisattva of craving-and-view compassion, not a real one. Venerable Miào Jìng: not abiding in nirvāṇa is great compassion; not abiding in saṃsāra is perfect wisdom.

quiz.q: How does Master Cháng Bǎi distinguish "harsh effort" from "forceful effort"?
options: bodily penalties like kneeling through an incense stick are harsh effort; verbal rebuke is forceful effort
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: correcting beings through bodily penalties, like making them kneel through an incense stick, is harsh effort; rebuking them verbally is forceful effort. Venerable Miào Jìng: the two are indeed different.

quiz.q: "Having wronged another, or being suspected of it … failing to apologise properly and dismissing it." What does each lecture emphasise?
options: Cháng Bǎi: pride makes it unequal — that is improper apology; Miào Jìng: even if you didn't wrong them, if they suspect you did, you should apologise
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: with pride there is no equality — that is called improper apology. Venerable Miào Jìng: even if you did not wrong them, if they suspect you did, you should apologise.
